entry.title: India must curb misleading health claims in booming nutraceuticals market
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Editorial / India must curb misleading health claims in booming nutraceuticals marketIndia must curb misleading health claims in booming nutraceuticals market

Misleading health claims in the growing nutraceutical market demand stricter regulation and stronger consumer protection

premium

The ASCI’s investigation found weight management to be the most prominent theme in advertisements, followed by skin care, anti-ageing, respiratory health and claims relating to specific diseases

Business Standard Editorial Comment3 min read Last Updated : Nov 19 2026 | 10:29 PM ISTThe Advertising Standards Council of India’s (ASCI’s) latest report, “A Pill for Thought”, highlights the risks of misleading health claims in India’s growing nutraceutical market. Of the 61 advertisements examined between July and September this year, all 60 completed cases violated the ASCI Code, while 31 advertisers failed to provide adequate evidence for their claims. The findings underline the need for stronger scrutiny of a market where false promises can have consequences for consumer health. The stakes are rising with the industry. According to one estimate, India’s nutraceutical market was valued at ₹3.67 trillion in 2025 and is projected to reach ₹8.05 trillion by 2033, growing at an annual rate of 10.3 per cent. Nutraceuticals, which include functional foods, fortified drinks, probiotics, vitamins and dietary supplements, occupy a space between food and pharmaceuticals. While these products can meet legitimate nutritional needs, their marketing must not exploit consumers’ health concerns.  The ASCI’s investigation found weight management to be the most prominent theme in advertisements, followed by skin care, anti-ageing, respiratory health and claims relating to specific diseases. Promises such as “Lose 6 kg in 60 days” and “Your thigh fat will be gone in 12 weeks” used before-and-after images to suggest predictable results. Some supplements and gummies positioned themselves as safer alternatives to prescription therapies. Such claims can create unrealistic expectations about the speed, extent and safety of the promised benefits. The problem extends beyond exaggerated weight-loss claims to claims reversing chronic diseases like asthma, obstructive pulmonary disease, blood pressure, cholesterol, and polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome.  The ASCI’s Annual Report for 2025-26 underlines the persistence of the problem. Nutraceuticals accounted for 52 per cent of food-and-beverage advertising cases, with 96 per cent requiring modification. The scale of violations suggests that existing mechanisms have not sufficiently deterred misleading claims. Although the ASCI’s self-regulatory framework can identify problematic advertisements and seek corrective action, its recommendations do not have the same force as statutory penalties. The rapid growth of digital advertising adds to the challenge. Influencers, sponsored content, and online marketplaces allow health claims to reach consumers quickly, often without the scrutiny applied to conventional advertisements.  India’s regulatory framework must, therefore, move beyond corrective action after an advertisement has appeared. The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) and Central Consumer Protection Authority need to strengthen enforcement against unsupported health claims. The recent FSSAI advisory on mandatory labelling requirements and warnings for botanical ingredients underlines the need for greater scrutiny of product composition and safety information. Advertisers should be required to maintain credible, product-specific scientific evidence before making claims, rather than relying on studies of individual ingredients. Independent testing and transparent disclosure of the evidence supporting health benefits can help improve accountability. Penalties must be proportionate to the scale of the violation and the potential harm to consumers. Repeated violations should attract stronger consequences rather than a request to modify an advertisement. Stronger regulation and scientific scrutiny are essential to ensure that products sold in the name of wellness deliver what they promise.     Topics : ASCI health Editorial Comment Business Standard Editorial Comment

entry.title: India must turn China trade dependence into domestic value addition
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Editorial / India must turn China trade dependence into domestic value additionIndia must turn China trade dependence into domestic value addition

India must balance dependence on Chinese imports with domestic manufacturing growth and better access to China's market

premium

The government has realised that India’s own industrial ambitions require a certain openness to specialised imports from China

Business Standard Editorial Comment4 min read Last Updated : Nov 19 2026 | 10:20 PM ISTIndia’s bilateral trade deficit with China continues to grow, in a manner that will concern New Delhi. According to the recent data, in the first seven months of 2026-27, it reached a record $83 billion, 30 per cent higher than in the same period the previous financial year. There is real concern that, over the entire year, it could reach $150 billion. In 2025-26, it had touched $112 billion. It is worth noting, however, that the time of knee-jerk protectionism against Chinese imports is, in general, past. The government has realised that India’s own industrial ambitions require a certain openness to specialised imports from China. India’s electronics production and exports, particularly of mobile phones, have grown considerably in the past year. Much of that growth is dependent upon being part of supply chains that require inputs made in China. It should be noted, therefore, that a growing trade deficit with one country, particularly when it dominates the manufacturing space the way China does, is not necessarily deleterious if it supports India’s own attempts to build a space for itself in manufacturing and other value chains.  The question the government should, thus, ask itself is whether domestic value addition is dependent on other countries and whether supplier ecosystems are emerging within the country at sufficient scale. If that is indeed happening, then at least some of the trade deficit is amply justified. The other question that needs asking is a more difficult one. As the Union finance minister said in Bangkok during the annual meetings of the World Bank and International Monetary Fund, the fundamental cause of the trade imbalance is that the Chinese market remains difficult to penetrate for Indian goods. She mentioned pharmaceuticals, among others, as a sector that was underperforming in terms of Indian exports to China.  This is not a problem that India alone faces. This is a global imbalance, caused by the fact that China’s state-led economy continues to artificially prioritise investment and production — and thus exports — over consumption. This is why its surplus in merchandise trade reached over $1 trillion in just the first 10 months of 2026, driven in part by growing exports of hi-tech goods that are needed to power the technological and artificial-intelligence transformation. If Chinese firms overinvest and create excess capacity, which then translates into low-cost exports, it is because the structure of their economy incentivises them to do so — through state support, directed credit, local-content preferences, and a slew of hidden and not-so-hidden subsidies. The weak purchasing power of Chinese households — caused by financial repression, quasi-administered wages, and an overdependence on the faltering real estate market as a store of wealth — doesn’t help.  This is not a problem, therefore, that New Delhi can easily solve on its own. It must continue to lobby for easier access to the Chinese market, but the bigger prize is to somehow speed up the internal transformation of the Chinese economy. This might require, in the end, multilateral efforts. It is unfortunate, however, that no attempt is being made at multilateral levels to directly address this. Leadership is required, and the natural candidate for it — the United States — is missing in action. President Donald Trump, who is now in China, is greatly concerned about trade imbalances but does not share this vision of how to address them. He would prefer to cut specific, sector-by-sector deals — but has so far largely failed to find any that stick. India must watch to see if any opening can be created for genuine multilateral action on this front — all while ensuring that its own unavoidable economic integration with China strengthens, and does not weaken, its position in global supply chains.     Topics : India china trade trade deficit China Indian exports Business Standard Editorial Comment Editorial Comment

entry.title: Women need equal access to P&L roles in order to reach boardrooms
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Editorial / Women need equal access to P&L roles in order to reach boardroomsWomen need equal access to P&L roles in order to reach boardrooms

Still, women account for less than 30.5 per cent in managerial positions globally

premium

A 2024 study found that requirement under the Companies Act for at least one woman director on board of a listed company reduced the share of firms with no women directors from 53% to below 10%

Business Standard Editorial Comment3 min read Last Updated : Nov 18 2026 | 9:33 PM ISTThe case for gender equality in the boardroom is becoming increasingly difficult for companies to ignore. However, efforts to translate this recognition into greater opportunities for women have been inadequate. The International Labour Organization’s (ILO’s) latest report, “Women in Business and Management: Scaling Success”, finds that 68.5 per cent of the enterprises globally reported improved business outcomes from gender equality and diversity initiatives in 2025, up from 57.4 per cent in 2018. Reported gains included better reputation, innovation, talent retention and profitability. Of enterprises reporting higher profits, 87.4 per cent recorded increases of at least 5 per cent.  Still, women account for less than 30.5 per cent in managerial positions globally. Their share in boards more than doubled, from 13.1 per cent in 2013 to 30.9 per cent in 2025, but progress lower down the hierarchy is less encouraging. Between 2013 and 2025, the share of enterprises achieving gender balance fell by 1.4 percentage points at junior management level and 6.4 percentage points at middle management. This weakens the pipeline from which future senior leaders are drawn. The problem is not only vertical exclusion. Women remain concentrated in human resources and administration. Consequently, 62.5 per cent and 55.4 per cent of the enterprises, respectively, reported women among senior managers in these functions. Their representation was far lower in profit-and-loss (P&L) roles (19.8 per cent) and research & development (26.3 per cent). These functions provide exposure to operations and strategy and often serve as the stepping-stone to executive positions. India’s record is particularly troubling. The ILO puts women’s share in managerial positions at fewer than 12 per cent, ranking India 32nd among 34 Asia-Pacific economies. Access to career-enhancing assignments is another constraint. A 2026 study of 1,500 leaders in India found that 49 per cent of the women leaders worked in enabling functions, compared with 37 per cent of the men. While 68 per cent of the women had P&L experience, the figure for the men was 91 per cent; only 45 per cent of the women had held sales roles, against 90 per cent of the men. Companies cannot expect more women at the top if they distribute key assignments unevenly.  A 2024 study found that the requirement under the Companies Act for at least one woman director on the board of a listed company reduced the share of firms with no women directors from 53 per cent to below 10 per cent. Having a woman on the board was associated with stronger economic performance and financial stability. However, positive employee sentiment was linked to board diversity only when women were also present in top management. In this context, it is worth mentioning that the ILO has identified an implementation gap. Although 74.8 per cent of the enterprises reported having an equal-opportunity or diversity policy, the average share implementing specific gender-equality initiatives fell from 37.4 per cent in 2018 to 26.5 per cent in 2025. Recruitment and promotion initiatives, leadership development, and mentoring recorded declines. Thus, commitments on paper are not enough. Companies should publish gender-disaggregated data, examine pay and promotion outcomes, create transparent career pathways, and give women equal access to P&L, sales and operational roles. At the same time, governments must improve access to child care, safe transport, and mechanisms to address workplace harassment to enable greater women labour force participation.     Topics : Gender equality women women on corporate boards Business Standard Editorial Comment Editorial Comment

entry.title: Quad summit reassures India but leaves its strategic role uncertain
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Editorial / Quad summit reassures India but leaves its strategic role uncertainQuad summit reassures India but leaves its strategic role uncertain

The Manila summit offers reassurance but does little to change the Quad's limited role in US geopolitical strategy

premium

Japanese PM Sanae Takaichi, PM Narendra Modi, US President Donald Trump and Australian PM Anthony Albanese pose for a group photograph during the Quad meeting in Manila, Philippines (Photo: Reuters)

Business Standard Editorial Comment3 min read Last Updated : Nov 18 2026 | 9:20 PM ISTThe remarkable flurry of summitry in Manila, Philippines, on November 17 — the 23rd India-Association of Southeast Asian Nations summit, the 21st East-Asia Summit, and the leader-level Quadrilateral Security Dialogue summit — did not significantly alter the region’s geo-economic dynamics. But it took place just days ahead of a historic trilateral summit between Presidents Donald Trump, Xi Jinping, and Vladimir Putin. Of these, the Quad meeting, comprising the leaders of the United States (US), Japan, India, and Australia, has been highlighted as a positive development for India and the Indo-Pacific powers. This could be an overstatement. For one, there is little evidence that the meeting significantly changed the direction of Indo-US relations, nor is there a dramatic departure in the Quad’s role. The statement that the Quad would “ensure open, safe and resilient maritime corridors in the Indo-Pacific” is a riff on an established theme. Most announcements listed in the short, joint press release — from cooperation on critical minerals to maritime surveillance, artificial intelligence, and cybersecurity cooperation — refer to ongoing projects. The exception is the Business Leaders’ Forum, scheduled to be held in Mumbai next year, but this, too, may be of less significance, given China’s overweening economic and technological dominance of and integration with the Indo-Pacific nations. It is, of course, reassuring for India that the meeting took place at all, given the current frictions in Indo-US relations. But it is noteworthy that the summit was held in Manila, the capital of Philippines, which is a partner in the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, a grouping that does not wholly approve of the Quad in the first place. China has long characterised the Quad as an “Indo-Pacific North Atlantic Treaty Organization” and has accused the US of fostering a Cold-War mentality by creating this grouping. This descriptor has acquired a fresh irony, given that the upcoming trilateral, expected to take place on November 19 on the sidelines of the China-led Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, is being portrayed by Western commentators as a second Yalta. The reference is to the post-World War II conference that defined spheres of influence in Europe between Joseph Stalin, Winston Churchill and Franklin Roosevelt. Seen against this backdrop, the timing of the Quad leaders’ summit — held nearly a decade after its formal founding in May 2007 in a non-member country — underlines its role as a tactical instrument for the US rather than a central component of its geopolitical strategy.  This much has been clear from the beginning. After a hopeful start in 2007, the grouping went into limbo until it was revived under US President Donald Trump in his first term. Leader-level summits, however, only took place for the first time in 2021, when Joe Biden as US President hosted a virtual summit. Five more summits followed, with the last being held in Wilmington, Delaware, in 2024. Thereafter, the 2025 summit, which was to be hosted in New Delhi, did not happen, a result of escalating tensions over trade and tariffs between the US and India. Although Quad foreign ministers continue to meet, the momentum appears to have slowed. The lack of clarity over the Quad’s role is underlined by the fact that though the next summit is expected to be held in New Delhi, no date has been set yet. That calendar may well be determined by the outcome at Shenzhen.     Topics : Quad Donald Trump Narendra Modi Indo-Pacific China Japan Business Standard Editorial Comment Editorial Comment

entry.title: India's lower health spending burden still masks gaps in public care
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Editorial / India's lower health spending burden still masks gaps in public careIndia's lower health spending burden still masks gaps in public care

Pharmaceuticals accounted for 30.2 per cent of current health expenditure, while outpatient curative care accounted for 19.3 per cent

premium

Private hospitals accounted for around 31.9 per cent of current health expenditure, almost twice the 15.9 per cent spent through government hospitals (Photo: AdobeStock)

Business Standard Editorial Comment3 min read Last Updated : Nov 17 2026 | 11:50 PM ISTThe latest estimates of the National Health Accounts (NHA) show India’s financing for health care has become less dependent on households, but this should not be mistaken for adequate public investment or universal financial protection. The share of out-of-pocket expenditure (OOPE) in total health spending indeed declined from 64.2 per cent in 2013-14 to 42.7 per cent in 2023-24. Over the same period, the government’s share rose from 28.6 per cent to 43.5 per cent. Government health expenditure increased to ₹4.14 trillion, nearly three times its level a decade earlier. These are significant shifts. But the increase is in nominal terms; more importantly, government health expenditure was only 1.43 per cent of gross domestic product in 2023-24, as against the National Health Policy 2017 target of 2.5 per cent by 2025. The target remains unmet.  At the same time, a lower OOPE share does not mean that households are no longer bearing a burden. Per capita OOPE rose from ₹2,767 in 2022-23 to ₹2,901 in 2023-24. The decline in the share must, therefore, be read alongside the absolute amount and the continuing risk of households incurring high costs when they need treatment. Insurance coverage also deserves attention in this context. The latest National Family Health Survey-6 (NFHS-6) fact sheet reports that 60.2 per cent of households had at least one usual member covered by a health-insurance or financing scheme in 2023-24, up from 41 per cent in NFHS-5. This is encouraging, but the indicator is household-based: It does not mean that 60.2 per cent of individuals have comprehensive insurance. The NHA estimates record ₹97,167 crore in private health-insurance expenditure and ₹33,385 crore under government-financed insurance schemes in 2023-24. The Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana (PM-JAY) provides up to ₹5 lakh per family for secondary and tertiary hospitalisation, but insurance-led protection does not automatically cover the costs of outpatient consultations, medicines and diagnostics.  The composition of health care spending points to why public provision remains central. Pharmaceuticals accounted for 30.2 per cent of current health expenditure, while outpatient curative care accounted for 19.3 per cent. These are expenses that can recur and weigh heavily on households. Private hospitals accounted for around 31.9 per cent of current health expenditure, almost twice the 15.9 per cent spent through government hospitals. Expanding insurance without adequate public facilities risks financing treatment in a system where private providers remain a bigger part of delivery. The Centre cannot meet this challenge alone and states accounted for about 68 per cent of government health expenditure in 2023-24. However, their fiscal capacity and health infrastructure vary considerably. Government spending is directed substantially towards primary care, which accounts for around 51 per cent of its current health expenditure, as it should. However, this must translate into functioning facilities, adequately staffed centres, reliable supplies of medicines, diagnostic services, and accessible outpatient care. The NHA numbers mark genuine progress in the way health care is financed. But a falling OOPE share needs to be seen in the overall context. The priority must be to raise public-health spending towards the stated target while strengthening primary care and public hospitals.     Topics : healthcare Expenditure Health Insurance Ayushman Bharat Business Standard Editorial Comment Editorial Comment

entry.title: 'Politics-proof' investment: Proposed Andhra law offers a template
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Editorial / 'Politics-proof' investment: Proposed Andhra law offers a template'Politics-proof' investment: Proposed Andhra law offers a template

Andhra Pradesh's investment protection law can provide policy stability and shield investors from arbitrary decisions by successive governments

premium

N Chandrababu Naidu, Chief Minister, Andhra Pradesh (Photo: PTI)

Business Standard Editorial Comment3 min read Last Updated : Nov 17 2026 | 11:43 PM ISTThe Andhra Pradesh government under N Chandrababu Naidu has offered states a progressive blueprint to attract and secure investors at a time when private-sector investment, Indian or foreign, has been thin on the ground. The Investment Protection Bill, to be introduced in the upcoming Assembly session, reflects the economic cost the state has paid due to the political rivalry of successive regimes. Prominent among them is the infamous “three capitals plan” of 2019, under which the YSR Congress Party government in the state decided to scrap the plan of the previous government, whose chief minister was, again, Mr Naidu, to establish a new capital, Amaravati, in the newly bifurcated state. Instead, the state was to have three separate capitals  — legislative, executive and judicial  — all located miles apart from one another. This plan reneged on the previous government’s commitment to compensate farmers who surrendered land for the single greenfield capital. Legal battles and parliamentary intervention sorted out the matter only in September 2026. The same YSR Congress regime also scrapped long-term power-purchase agreements in renewable energy with retrospective effect, an issue that worked its way through the courts till 2022. The law concerned shields investment by ensuring that future governments cannot arbitrarily cancel or alter valid commitments. To this end, the law covers land allotment, water pricing, fiscal and non-fiscal incentives, infrastructure support and regulatory approvals. Significantly, the state also plans to introduce an escrow account to guarantee the timely delivery of industrial incentives, though it is unclear how this will function since the law is still in the drafting stage. Announced at the 31st Confederation of Indian Industry Partnership Summit in Visakhapatnam, the state government is seeking broader support from New Delhi for a National Investment Protection Act. The Concurrent List of the Constitution allows states to enact legislation of this nature but neither the states nor the Centre has such laws in place.  The chronic variability of policymaking under different political administrations suggests that states hoping to attract investment would do well to follow Andhra Pradesh’s example rather than wait for a model national law. In West Bengal, for example, the Trinamool Congress government’s arbitrary decisions to review compensation for land losers in the Tata-Nano project or the cancellation, with retrospective effect, of three decades of industrial commitments, subsidies, and other concessions played stellar roles in the further flight of industry.  The major issue, perhaps, is how far successive governments will genuinely honour the letter and spirit of such a law. Inasmuch as all laws are subject to legal challenges, the risk of investors being subjected to lengthy lawsuits by successor regimes  — a major pain point  — remains. This is a key reason India’s key economic partners, for example, are demanding a one-year window for the exhaustion of legal remedies in arbitration contracts under bilateral-investment treaties rather than the government’s reported offer of three years. Though a stable investment environment can only be as “politics-proof” as the politicians will allow, an investment-protection law will offer a degree of predictability that has been elusive in India’s economic landscape.     Topics : N Chandrababu Naidu Andhra Pradesh Investment Business Standard Editorial Comment Editorial Comment

entry.title: Beyond the Jan Dhan Passbook
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / Beyond the Jan Dhan PassbookBeyond the Jan Dhan Passbook

Banks deepen financial inclusion when they align earnings, livelihoods and risk protection through patient hand-holding

premium

ILLUSTRATION: Ajaya Kumar Mohanty

Tamal Bandyopadhyay8 min read Last Updated : Nov 22 2026 | 12:17 PM ISTIn January 2025, South Andaman's official newsletter recorded a visit by senior administrators to a Jarawa settlement at Jirkatang to hand over voter identity cards to 19 members of the tribe, marking the Jarawa's first inclusion in the electoral roll. It was an electoral exercise, not a banking camp. Yet, it carries a lesson for every public institution: Service must move towards people, not wait for people to find it.  Another archival record, a presentation hosted by the National Commission for Scheduled Tribes, notes that insurance premiums were paid for 32 Onge individuals under the Janashree Bima Yojana from 2007, alongside livelihood support through the Onge Multi-Purpose Cooperative Society.  Such episodes capture what financial inclusion ought to mean: Recognition, access and protection tailored to how people actually live.  The finance ministry's Nationwide Financial Inclusion Saturation Campaign, running from 21 October to 31 December, gives India's banking system another chance to put that principle into practice. Steered by the Department of Financial Services (DFS), the drive covers 270,000 gram panchayats and urban local bodies across the country.  Going beyond account opening, camps run by banks, led by public sector lenders, are tackling a set of operational bottlenecks: Re-KYC (know your customer) for Jan Dhan and regular savings accounts, pending Central KYC identifiers, nomination updates for accounts and lockers, revival of inoperative accounts, and enrolment under the micro-insurance and pension schemes.  Former Reserve Bank of India (RBI) Governor Y V Reddy coined the phrase "financial inclusion" while drafting the annual policy statement for 2006-07, released in April 2006, with Deputy Governor Usha Thorat. The term may have arrived in 2006, but Indian banking's push into the hinterland began in the late 1960s, with bank nationalisation and directed credit to neglected sectors and weaker sections. In the 1970s, the RBI laid down priority sector lending norms; experiments followed with regional rural banks, the self-help group–bank linkage programme and local area banks.  The current campaign is different in design. It is about fixing the plumbing of existing accounts.  In West Bengal, the State Level Bankers' Committee (SLBC) is working with member banks, district administrations, panchayats and municipalities, with a sharp focus on households from Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Groups.  In Punjab, SLBC convenor Punjab National Bank, peer lenders and district collectors are prioritising the revival of inoperative accounts across 13,236 village panchayats and 166 urban local bodies, backed by 7,669 bank branches and 98 financial literacy centres.  RBI Governor Sanjay Malhotra on Saturday inaugurated a special financial inclusion camp at Vaksai in Maharashtra,  organised by Bank of Maharashtra. It focuses on re-KYC of bank accounts and expanding access to banking services.   Meanwhile, State Bank of India, which is the SLBC convenor in Assam and its neighbouring states, is steering the drive across Assam, Arunachal Pradesh, Manipur, Meghalaya, Mizoram, Nagaland and Tripura.  At the North-East Bankers' Conclave 3.0, held in Aizawl in October, the government reported that banks had opened 131 branches and installed 126 ATMs in the region between December 2024 and March 2026, and that 6,905 of 9,479 identified villages were now connected to either a bank branch or an India Post Payments Bank (IPPB) outlet. This progress predates the current drive. Of the remaining 2,574 villages, 2,515 will be linked through IPPB and 59 through brick-and-mortar branches.  The next phase of that expansion rests on a crucial regulatory tweak, announced at the same conclave. Elsewhere in India, the guideline for opening a brick-and-mortar branch requires a minimum population of 3,000. In the North-East, where difficult terrain and scattered hamlets make single-village thresholds unworkable, that norm has been lowered to 2,000 and applied on a cluster basis, allowing banks to pool adjacent villages to justify a central branch.  Yet bricks-and-mortar alone is not enough. Physical reach must be matched by explanations in the local language and reliable follow-up. The best camp is one where visitors walk away understanding both the service they received and their next step.  For communities such as the Jarawa and the Onge of the Andaman Islands, inclusion must also respect distinct social identities. Policy towards the Jarawa rightly emphasises protection from intrusive outside contact and the preservation of their social structure, subsistence and culture. In September 2025, the islands' cooperative newsletter noted that the Andaman and Nicobar State Cooperative Bank has 41 branches across 14 islands, while highlighting the role of Ellon Hinengo Ltd and the Tribal Development Cooperative Society in fostering tribal economic self-reliance.  On the ground, practical questions decide whether inclusion sticks. Who explains the form, corrects a clerical error and stays reachable after the camp packs up? Banks deepen inclusion only when they align earnings, livelihoods and risk protection through patient hand-holding, never through target-driven enrolment pressure.  Launched on 28 August 2014, the Pradhan Mantri Jan-Dhan Yojana (PMJDY) remains the bedrock passbook of this effort. As of 4 November 2026, PMJDY had 597 million beneficiaries, 333 million of them women and 463.4 million banked at rural and semi-urban branches. Together they hold Rs3.28 trillion in deposits and 419 million RuPay cards. Public sector banks carry the bulk of the load with 459 million accounts, while regional rural banks hold another 112 million.  Now consider how the camp priorities are trying to make those accounts work harder.  To ease re-KYC friction, the RBI in June 2025 allowed banks to use authorised business correspondents to collect self-declarations from customers whose KYC details are unchanged or where only the address has changed, subject to safeguards, while keeping the bank accountable for completing the update.  For dormant money, the RBI's UDGAM (Unclaimed Deposits – Gateway to Access inforMation) portal lets citizens search for unclaimed balances across banks in one place. Deposits left unclaimed for 10 years move to the Depositor Education and Awareness Fund, yet depositors or their legal heirs can claim them at any time, with no time limit.  Social security forms the next pillar. The Pradhan Mantri Jeevan Jyoti Bima Yojana (PMJJBY) offers life cover of Rs 2 lakh for death from any cause at an annual premium of Rs 436. Open to account holders aged 18 to 50 and renewable up to the age of 55, it is a pure term cover with no maturity value, and new or rejoining subscribers face a 30-day waiting period for deaths other than by accident. By 22 July 2026, cumulative enrolments stood at 280.6 million with over 1 million claims settled up to 30 June 2026.  Along with it, the Pradhan Mantri Suraksha Bima Yojana (PMSBY) gives account holders aged 18 to 70 a cover of Rs 2 lakh for accidental death or permanent total disability (and Rs 1 lakh for permanent partial disability) for Rs 20 a year. Cumulative enrolments reached 591 million by 22 July 2026, with 189,057 claims disbursed up to 30 June 2026. Crucially, PMSBY is an accident cover, not a health policy; it does not reimburse hospital bills.  Both schemes rely on consent-based auto-debit and annual renewal. Consent matters because a family that knows a policy exists is far more likely to file a timely claim. Rather than touting cumulative enrolments alone, banks and insurers should publish the number of active policies, renewal success rates and lapses. Debiting a premium from a Jan Dhan account does not automatically translate into effective protection.  Can a bereaved family identify the insurer, recognise the premium debit in a passbook and navigate the claim paperwork? Banks' duty of care must extend to renewal alerts, minimum-balance reminders, help with documentation and claim channels that people can understand.  Similarly, the Atal Pension Yojana (APY) guarantees a minimum monthly pension of between Rs 1,000 and Rs 5,000 after the age of 60 to citizens who join between the ages of 18 and 40, do not pay income tax and contribute regularly until retirement. As of 8 November 2026, APY had 81 million active subscribers and Rs 60,299 crore in assets under management. Because APY is a long-term contributory commitment, not a free dole, bankers must explain contribution obligations and exit rules clearly before signing anyone up.  The Jarawa electoral roll was an act of civic recognition, not an insurance drive. But its lesson for banking is unmistakable: Institutions earn trust when they listen, return and see the job through, turning financial inclusion from a form-filling exercise into an enduring relationship.  _____________________________________________________________________________________________________ The writer is an author and senior advisor to Jana Small Finance Bank Ltd. His latest book: Roller Coaster: An Affair with Banking. To read his previous columns, log on to www.bankerstrust.in. X: @TamalBandyo         Disclaimer: These are personal views of the writer. entry.title: India Inc must summon the courage to challenge government policy openly
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / India Inc must summon the courage to challenge government policy openlyIndia Inc must summon the courage to challenge government policy openly

One big cause of Mr Modi's frustration is corporate India's unwillingness to pass on the benefits of tax cuts to employees through raises, hiring, or investment

Prime Minister Narendra Modi addresses the inaugural session of FICCI’s Annual General Meeting and Annual Convention. | Image credit: FICCI (X)

Shekhar Gupta7 min read Last Updated : Nov 21 2026 | 10:12 AM ISTThe most apt description for Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s mass admonition of corporate India at the Ficci annual general meeting is that it was a cri de coeur. I use this even as I’m reminded of the late and venerable D N Singh, my first news editor at The Indian Express in 1977. He had banned “foreign” words in our writing. English is foreign enough for all of us, he’d say. In this case, however, a cry from the heart doesn’t fully capture where the Prime Minister was coming from. The dictionary tells us that a cri de coeur is more profound. It’s a “passionate, heartfelt appeal, protest, even an outcry”. The Prime Minister spoke in anger, frustration, helplessness even. What more can I do to get you guys moving? It was way more fraught than a mere cry from the heart.  It’s a bit like a general failing to implore his troops to assault a hill despite a thousand war cries, words of inspiration, even a dash of “spirit”. Since we started with a bit of French, that “spirit” reference is from the Duke of Wellington at the Battle of Waterloo. While his original line, as recorded in history, was less dramatic, Christopher Plummer, playing Wellington in the 1970 film Waterloo, tells the Duchess of Richmond, who wants to know where his troops get their inspiration to fight: “Gin is the spirit of their patriotism.” I’m avoiding the full quote because the Prime Minister certainly didn’t want to call corporate India ‘scum, beggars and scoundrels,’ as Wellington called his troops. It’s just that his frustration is as profound.

Also Read

Doing our bit: India Inc responds to PM's wake-up call on jobs and pay

PM 'rattled', realised he will be 'outgoing PM' soon, says Congress

Nepal PM's 2-day India visit: Rail link, trading post on the cards

Technology created vistas for cultural connectivity, says PM Modi

Wife brand vs Mistress Brand: Can public status outweigh private utility?premium

 What’s the spirit that a government can offer entrepreneurship? It can be many things: Deregulation, minimum government, fair market supervision, fiscal discipline, freedom from licensing and investment restrictions. And certainly, the gin equivalent of this “spiritual” package would be tax cuts. One big cause of Mr Modi’s frustration is corporate India’s unwillingness to pass this benefit on to employees through raises, hiring or investment. This hasn’t happened even as corporate profits have risen. These troops are unwilling, either too scared to assault that hill or simply too comfortable in safety, pocketing the tax breaks. Let’s read some of Mr Modi’s words to Ficci. “In 2014, the basic corporate tax rate was 30 per cent. We reduced it to 22 per cent. Today, there’s no income tax on earnings up to ~12 lakh in India.” And then he turns the knife. “I know you won’t clap, because however much one gives, your appetite never seems to be satisfied. (aap ka pet nahin bharta). Did you increase the salaries of your employees? Did you increase the number of employees? No. The attitude remains: ‘Modi ji, you do it, we will see’.” While India Inc was left licking its wounded pride, the Congress quickly latched on to the Prime Minister’s words. Isn’t this what we’ve been saying all along, it hit back. Jairam Ramesh was first out of the blocks. “For the first time in 12 years, a nervous and rattled PM has pulled up the captains of industry... (who) must have been taken aback and shocked.” In an elaborate post on X, he blamed not businesses but the government for this stall. He blamed it on crony capitalism, regulatory capture, “an atmosphere of fear and intimidation”, and the unleashing of “investigative agencies”. He concluded by suggesting the Prime Minister look inwards. Rahul Gandhi, on his speaking tour in the United States, also said: We told you so. It’s not my place here to hold forth on the state of the economy. But we know corporate India hasn’t been investing, expanding and hiring, at least nowhere near what 7 per cent-plus growth would indicate. Startups are rising, but largely there’s an entrepreneurship freeze. Much of the growth comes from government spending, especially in heavy infrastructure. If corporate India looks so risk-averse, this isn’t a sudden development. The mood has been festering for years. Some complain of a lack of demand, others say regulation is asphyxiating. Still too many forms need to be filled for too many small things, even something as virtuous as exports. Because, I suppose, the Reserve Bank of India wants to track every dollar that comes in. And, of course, everything in triplicate please. The government may have loosened policies here and there, but the bureaucratic grip is tighter than before. A quick quiz, and no Googling. Can you name the ministers of mines, pharmaceuticals and steel? I mention these three because the Prime Minister highlighted corporate India’s failures specifically in these areas. Why do we export raw materials like iron ore, have so much bauxite, yet import finished steel and specialised aluminium alloys? How come, despite robust pharma exports, we remain dependent on China for APIs, or active pharmaceutical ingredients? With key ministers too lightweight or distracted by party work, and power centralised in the PMO, which is obviously far too overburdened to attend to everything, discretion devolves to the bureaucracies. Corporate India is resigned to this. It’s buying peace in the manner it knows best: Distributing some of the spoils in a way that’s entirely legal and above board, but also revealing. Check out the number of retiring secretaries, especially in the finance ministry, finding sinecures on the boards of influential companies and as chairpersons of almost all significant private-sector banks, and the recently listed stock market titan, NSE (National Stock Exchange). The more the Modi government thinks it’s reforming — and reforming it is — the more it does so in a way that passes power into the hands of the bureaucracy. Corporate India buys peace with them in advance, merely by dropping hints. Here’s the paradox. This is a super-strong government with a very weak implementation spine. As a result, what’s decentralised at the top gathers in the middle. A strong government isn’t immune to policy confusion. On the contrary, it can be prone to flip-flop-flips given its overwhelming power. Long term capital gains (LTCG) tax is a big discussion point now. Count how many changes this government has brought in. The same goes for taxes on dividends. Since 1991, successive finance ministers have said that the essence of a reformed economy lies in moderate, predictable taxes. You most certainly cannot say the same about this government, which also taxes individuals at almost twice the rate of corporations. It’s also been breathtaking in its use of sovereign power. A striking example is the retrospective changes it made to sovereign gold bonds to suit itself and cover for those brilliant people who floated these without hedging for gold prices. The message is an old one. In India, the government, the almighty Sarkar-e-Hind, can never be wrong. Corporate India has a lot to answer for, but for some, the chappal is on the government’s foot. On copper and aluminium imports, two of the largest projects have been shut under activist pressure. If this government has failed to move on these, it cannot blame India Inc. Sadly, corporate India knows this, but nobody would dare speak up. They whisper dark things on the sidelines. But in front of an angry Prime Minister, or the finance minister who’s been delivering the same admonitions for two years, they sit silent and contrite, like schoolkids whose homework the dog ate. This isn’t just a Modi-era phenomenon. At the 2007 CII AGM, then Prime Minister Manmohan Singh had chided corporate leaders for paying themselves too much. The irony: The mood and message then were opposite to now. Sunil Mittal, then CII chief, responded by pledging ‘a significant part of his salary bonus’ to charity. I had then written, and repeated in a 2013 column, that corporate India has to grow the spine to tell the Prime Minister he didn’t fix their wages. He should leave them alone if they paid their taxes honestly. Of course, no such thing happened. Corporate India also swallowed that retrograde idea of near-mandatory corporate social responsibility. Even at Ficci, and in the corporate and financial universe, too many good people have too many important points to make. But nobody would dare. Corporate India is waiting for its next Rahul Bajaj. Or preferably a few of them.

entry.title: India needs flexible corporate rules that move beyond box-ticking
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / India needs flexible corporate rules that move beyond box-tickingIndia needs flexible corporate rules that move beyond box-ticking

India's muscular regulatory regime should make room for alternative governance practices, allowing companies to show a different route to the same goal

premium

Representative image of a corporate board meeting discussing governance and compliance

Amit Tandon5 min read Last Updated : Nov 17 2026 | 11:52 PM ISTWhen the Companies Act, 2013, made corporate social responsibility (CSR) a legal obligation, India briefly allowed companies to explain their non-compliance. Boards were to ensure at least 2 per cent of average net profits went to CSR, but a company that fell short faced no penalty. It only had to give its reasons in the board’s report.  That experiment in “comply or explain” is over. Since January 2021, unspent money must be moved to a dedicated account or a government fund, with penalties of up to twice the amount, capped at ₹1 crore. Boards still explain a shortfall, but they need to spend the amount.  The shift fits a pattern. India regulates companies mostly by command. The Companies Act and Sebi (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations 2015 (LODR) prescribe board composition, committees, approval of related-party transactions and disclosures, with penalties for breach. This “comply or else” model offers clear rules and an enforcer with teeth. But rules mean boards learn to satisfy the letter rather than the purpose. A 2014 NSE briefing by Nawshir Mirza and Nirmal Mohanty observed that Indian governance norms were “practised more as rituals in religion than as a genuine pursuit of good governance”.  Mandates also leave regulators few options when a rule meets resistance. In February 2022, weeks before India’s top 500 listed companies had to separate the roles of chairperson and managing director or chief executive officer, the Securities and Exchange Board of India (Sebi) found only about half had complied. Rather than penalising a large slice of the market, it made the rule voluntary. It could instead have retained the mandate while allowing companies that chose to keep a combined role to explain their reasons to shareholders annually.  Much of the world uses that softer toolkit. Britain adopted “comply or explain” in 1992, following the Cadbury Committee. A code sets out principles and practices. A company may depart from a practice if it explains why publicly, and shareholders, not the regulator, judge the explanation. Variants have followed:  l Apply or explain (South Africa’s King III code, named after Mervyn King, and the Dutch code): Apply the principles and explain how. l Apply and explain (South Africa’s King IV code, UK Stewardship Code): No opt-out; show how each principle is applied. l Report or explain: Publish data, such as sustainability or diversity metrics, or explain why not. l Comply and explain: A mandate plus a narrative, as India’s CSR regime now works. l Opt in or opt out: Sets a default and lets companies choose a different path. Example, the European Union Takeover Directive’s rule that bars boards from frustrating a bid, which member states can opt out of and companies can opt-back in. l If not, why not, is Australia’s version and deserves a closer look.    “If not, why not” works like comply or explain, but differs in emphasis. “Comply or explain” makes compliance the default, so an explanation can read like an excuse. “If not, why not” treats not adopting a recommendation as a decision the board is entitled to make. The Australian Securities Exchange’s principles state that a board that considers a recommendation unsuited to its circumstances is entitled not to adopt it. Companies must give their reasons and say what they do instead. That pushes them to show a different route to the same goal, not just a gap. The approach has lasted two decades, and the draft fifth edition of the principles keeps it.  India has used these tools mainly as a glide path. Besides CSR, Sebi’s rule that large companies raise a quarter of their incremental borrowing through bonds ran on comply or explain for two years before penalties applied. Value-chain disclosures under BRSR Core began as “comply or explain” in 2023 and became voluntary in 2025. The LODR’s list of “discretionary” requirements asks for no explanation at all.  India should ask “if not, why not”.The NSE briefing argued comply or explain needs boards that value good governance, honest explanations and investors who act on them. CSR adds a lesson: Explanation works only where someone has a reason to read it. CSR benefits society rather than shareholders, so investors had little incentive to challenge thin explanations. Today’s domestic funds and insurers, bound by stewardship codes and supported by proxy advisers, are better placed to use it.  Sebi could start by turning the LODR’s “discretionary” norms into “if not, why not” requirements. Companies would report against them, and against others issues such as a separate chairperson, limits on director tenure and board diversity, explaining any departure and the alternative they had adopted. For new disclosures like value-chain emissions, “report or explain” would be better than swinging between mandate and retreat. New mandates could be phased in with a comply-or-explain period, as the bond-borrowing rule was. Hard law should remain for the core: Related-party transactions, audit, minority protection and disclosure of material events.  Explanations need policing too. Britain’s Financial Reporting Council reviews companies’ corporate governance reporting annually and calls out boilerplate explanations. Sebi or the exchanges could do the same, but would need to build the necessary capacity.  Mandatory rules set a floor, and India needs such floors — on board structure, pay, succession and disclosure quality. Investors have a stake. But CSR shows India will mandate when explanations fail. It should be as willing to move the other way when a mandate becomes a ritual. More flexible regulations will help boards move beyond box-ticking towards governing.

entry.title: Budget may stay within deficit goal, but spending plans need realism
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / Budget may stay within deficit goal, but spending plans need realismBudget may stay within deficit goal, but spending plans need realism

Worrying about fiscal deficit is fine, but meeting spending targets is more important

premium

Illustration: Binay Sinha

A K Bhattacharya New Delhi 7 min read Last Updated : Nov 17 2026 | 11:49 PM ISTConsultations with stakeholders for the upcoming Union Budget began this week. Fourteen rounds of such discussions will take place until November 26. Perhaps reflecting the political mood, the finance ministry has decided to hold consultations also with GenZ representatives, including students and young professionals. Economists and farm-sector representatives have already urged the finance ministry to stick to its debt reduction goal despite expenditure pressure, review the government’s stance on long-term capital gains tax without necessarily abolishing it only for foreign investors, improve the targeting of fertiliser subsidies, and ease priority-sector lending norms as well as procedures for importing cattle feed ingredients that are in short supply. The Budget exercise has truly begun.  What Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman will present on February 1, 2027, will be her ninth consecutive Union Budget (excluding one interim Budget). Quite apart from the fact that the 2027-28 Budget will make Ms Sitharaman the finance minister to have produced the most Union Budgets, it will also present perhaps her biggest challenge: Maintaining fiscal prudence while propping up the growth engine to benefit all sections of society. Concerns over demand and investments have become as important as the challenges arising from jobs and wages. Official numbers on unemployment show a marginal decline, along with an increase in the labour force participation rate, but real wages have either stagnated or even fallen for a large number of workers in the last decade. External sector problems look a little more manageable with the recent decline in international crude-oil prices, but a widening trade deficit in merchandise goods reflects weaknesses afflicting manufacturing and exporting firms, particularly those in the medium and small sector.    Data for the Union government’s revenue and expenditure during the first half of 2026-27 is available. A look at these numbers points to a few worrying signals. Questions are bound to arise regarding the Union government’s ability to meet its fiscal deficit target of 4.3 per cent of gross domestic product (GDP) in 2026-27.  Tepid growth in net tax revenue in the first half of the current year at less than 4 per cent is the first cause of concern. The full-year’s net tax revenue growth target was over 9 per cent. Non-tax revenues and miscellaneous non-debt capital receipts (or revenue from disinvestment and asset monetisation) have done well. Non-tax revenues grew by 3 per cent even though the full-year’s projection under this head envisaged no increase, while receipts from disinvestment more than doubled against a much lower target of increasing it by about 35 per cent. However, this is no real comfort. Non-tax revenues and disinvestment receipts account for less than a fifth of the government’s total projected non-debt receipts for 2026-27.  A bigger concern is the pace of expenditure growth in the first half of the current year. Against an annual budgeted target of 9 per cent, the growth in the government’s total expenditure was close to 11 per cent. Growth in revenue expenditure was about 10 per cent, against the annual target of less than 8 per cent, and capital expenditure in the first half of 2026-27 grew by 13 per cent, a shade lower than the annual target of 14 per cent. This is not a healthy sign, particularly when private-sector investments have not yet gained the desired momentum.  The government’s fiscal performance in the first half of 2026-27 reveals yet another problem. At the start of the year, it had announced a brave plan to cut subsidies by about 10 per cent over what was spent in 2025-26, although it was not clear how that reduction would be achieved. Even if there were some plans to cut subsidies, those were dashed about a month after the Budget was presented, when the war in West Asia led to a blockade in the Strait of Hormuz, through which about a fourth of global crude oil and gas supplies pass.  Not only did international crude-oil prices spike, but even supplies of oil and gas were adversely affected. Fertiliser prices too shot up. This poured cold water on the government’s plans to cut its major subsidies, almost 45 per cent of which are accounted for by fertilisers and petroleum products. Prices of crude oil and fertilisers have now fallen and stabilised. But even before prices came down, the government managed its fertiliser subsidies quite well. In the first half of 2026-27, fertiliser subsidy growth was restricted to 11 per cent (largely due to linking fertiliser sales to farmers’ land holdings with the help of Agristack and other similar digital platforms) and even the growth in the food subsidies bill was reined in at about 17 per cent.    Remember that the petroleum subsidies bill was kept under check because the oil companies absorbed the impact of higher crude-oil prices, helped as they were by the government move to reduce excise duty on petroleum products, mainly petrol and diesel. State-controlled oil companies took a hit as a result, as did the government’s net tax revenues and prospects of dividend income from them. Going forward, this cannot be good news for the Union government’s fiscal consolidation plan.  Already, the government’s fertiliser subsidies bill by the second week of November 2026 has reportedly risen to ₹1.46 trillion, almost 85 per cent of the budgeted allocation under this head for the full year. It is clear that the government’s major subsidies outlay of ₹4.1 trillion will be exceeded by a good margin by the time the current year ends. With net tax revenues growth a little subdued and expenditure slippages almost certain, can the government meet its fiscal deficit target of 4.3 per cent of GDP? To its credit, the government has in the past few years generally refrained from seeking recourse to imaginative accounting techniques, and instead embraced transparent accounting practices. Hopefully, the government will continue to stay on course in this regard. More importantly, however, the government may not be under any pressure to employ such techniques as issuing oil bonds many years ago or tapping extra budgetary resources through fully-serviced government bonds until five years ago. This is because the government’s own ability to spend the resources allocated by it during the year is limited. Over the years, its absorptive capacity to spend the entire money allocated under various important schemes has remained poor. In 2025-26, actual total expenditure by the government was about 3 per cent short of what was budgeted at the start of the year. If a similar saving of 3 per cent is achieved in 2026-27, the government would enjoy an expenditure cushion of about ₹1.6 trillion. This could absorb a good part of the likely revenue shortfall (which will be lower because of a sharp increase in disinvestment receipts) and even the slippage in subsidies expenditure.  Two messages emerge from this. One, the government should not be unduly worried about its performance on the fiscal consolidation front. Even though its revenues do not match up to its targets and subsidies bill exceeds the budgeted amount, it will continue to enjoy the benefit of expenditure savings and keep the fiscal deficit from becoming much wider than the target. Two, while preparing the 2027-28 Budget, it should be more focused on instilling a degree of realism and pragmatism in preparing its expenditure plan. An economy that needs to grow faster requires more investment and proper expenditure planning, particularly in key infrastructure areas.     Disclaimer: These are personal views of the writer. entry.title: India's labour Codes at one: From reform to results, what has changed?
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / India's labour Codes at one: From reform to results, what has changed?India's labour Codes at one: From reform to results, what has changed?

India's labour Codes must move from regulatory reform to effective implementation, ensuring better worker protection and ease of doing business

premium

Importantly, the labour Codes lay the foundation for extending social security coverage to unorganised, gig and platform workers (Photo: Shutterstock)

Sumita Dawra5 min read Last Updated : Nov 17 2026 | 11:04 PM ISTA year ago, on November 21 2025, the government notified the labour Codes, marking one of India’s most comprehensive labour reforms since Independence. Nearly five years after Parliament passed the Codes in 2019-2020, the government moved towards implementation, having engaged with stakeholders in the intervening period to undertake preparatory work and clarify  key provisions. With the focus now shifting to execution, it is timely to take stock of the progress made during the first year and consider what more needs to be done to ensure that the reforms deliver their intended outcomes.  A significant development, first and foremost, has been the progress towards a common regulatory framework, replacing the complex web of statutes and compliance requirements that historically discouraged business expansion. While addressing stakeholder concerns is an ongoing process, a near-uniform acceptance of the codes is evident.   From notification to operationalisation of rules  Following notification, several procedural and compliance provisions of the Codes required detailed rules. Therefore, the government published the draft Central rules under all four Codes on 30 December 2025, inviting stakeholder comments and suggestions. Following the consultation process, final Central rules under all four Codes were notified in May 2026.  With labour on the concurrent list, states and union territories must also notify rules within their jurisdictions. At the state level, the process of framing and notifying corresponding rules has progressed at varying speeds. While some states and union territories have notified final rules under all four Codes, others are at final stages of rule-making.  Digital compliance and ease of doing business  Digital compliance is a key driver of ease of doing business (EoDB). The labour ministry has launched the revamped Shram Suvidha 2.0 portal in recent months, enabling businesses to obtain a single registration, secure a single licence and file a single return, thereby simplifying compliance across labour authorities.  A pragmatic approach appears to allow states to retain their existing digital compliance systems rather than requiring their integration into a single Central portal. For businesses operating across multiple states, Shram Suvidha is expected to serve as a common interface for coordinated compliance and time-bound approvals.  Building a wider social security ecosystem  Importantly, the labour Codes lay the foundation for extending social security coverage to unorganised, gig and platform workers. In a significant step towards operationalising this framework, the Union government, on 30 October 2026, notified the constitution of two separate National Social Security Boards — one for unorganised workers and the other for gig and platform workers.   The Boards are mandated to recommend, advise on and monitor welfare schemes for these categories of workers, thereby paving the way for more inclusive social security coverage and strengthening the formalisation of India’s workforce. Further, the e-Shram portal’s aggregator module continues to facilitate the registration and integration of platform workers into the social security framework, representing an important dimension of extending social security coverage to the gig and platform economy.  What has changed for workers and businesses?  As implementation progresses, the labour Codes are beginning to deliver tangible benefits for workers and businesses. For workers, a key reform is the uniform definition of wages, establishing a minimum 50 per cent wage base for calculating social security contributions and other statutory benefits. Industry practitioners indicate that most large enterprises have undertaken wage restructuring and made necessary financial provisions.  Two other illustrative indications from the field concern maternity benefits and payment of wages. In both areas, the Codes have expanded the Central government’s jurisdiction. Increased representations reportedly received by Central labour authorities in these areas suggest greater awareness and use of these mechanisms.  Apart from digital compliance mechanisms being in place, the inspector-cum-facilitator system defined under the Codes brings relief to businesses. It seeks to replace the traditional inspection-heavy approach with risk-based oversight, digital reporting and an emphasis on self-compliance.   EPFO reforms and expansion of formal social security  Meanwhile, the Employees’ Provident Fund Organisation (EPFO) has strengthened the formal social security framework by notifying its schemes in June 2026. Effective 17 September 2026, the mandatory EPFO wage ceiling also increased from  ₹15,000 to ₹25,000 per month, extending provident fund, pension and insurance coverage to more employees.  Additionally, the VISHWAS and AMNESTY schemes, notified in June 2026, signal a shift towards facilitation rather than enforcement alone.  What stakeholders expect next  Stakeholders may continue to require handholding, clarity and predictability in the implementation process for some time. Key priorities would include timely state-level notifications, effective grievance redressal mechanisms, operationalisation of the floor wage framework, a single point of contact for resolving EPF-related issues, early notification of social security schemes for the unorganised sector, to name a few.   Representatives of the construction industry have suggested an integrated labour database or a ‘labour stack’ that could play a critical role in enabling portability of benefits, ensuring continuity of coverage and preventing duplication.  The road ahead: From reform to delivery  Ultimately, the Codes’ success will be measured by outcomes, some of these being: Wage related, greater female labour force participation, safer workplaces, greater formalisation of India’s labour market, a predictable compliance environment with enhanced transparency and simplification of processes for greater EoDB.
